claims.text: Adding approximately 2–3 at.% Zr during synthesis will improve glass-forming ability in phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
Adding approximately 2–3 at.% Zr will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
Zr induces local atomic rearrangements that promote medium-range topological disorder.
Zr-induced atomic rearrangements frustrate the nucleation of crystalline phases.
The atomic-size mismatch and chemical affinity of Zr disrupt the short- and medium-range order required for crystal nucleation during cooling.
Trace Zr reduces atomic mobility in the alloy.
Trace Zr lowers the driving force for crystallization.
Reduced atomic mobility and a lower crystallization driving force increase the stability of the amorphous phase.
The Zr-modified alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation than the Zr-free baseline.
The Zr-modified alloy will have a higher glass-transition temperature than the Zr-free baseline.
The Zr-modified alloy will have a higher crystallization temperature than the Zr-free baseline.
The intervention should work under rapid melt-quenching when processing conditions are otherwise identical between Zr-containing and control samples.
The intervention should be effective when the baseline alloy does not already contain elements having atomic-size-mismatch and chemical effects comparable to Zr.
The beneficial effect exists only within a narrow Zr-composition window.
Excessive Zr may promote phase separation or crystallization rather than improve glass formation.
Significantly different base compositions may not exhibit the proposed improvement.
Slower cooling may eliminate the proposed improvement or promote crystallization.
